clue.text: Bad habits take a grip

definitions.meaning: ..., used as a mass noun, means wicked habits or immoral conduct in general
a bench tool with jaws that grips work firmly

explanation.surface: Someone with bad habits is told to get a grip on themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' is only a link joining the two senses; the plural 'habits' is covered because vice as a mass noun covers many bad habits.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: wickedness as a general failing, and a clamping tool on a workbench.

clue.text: Is that all you can say?

definitions.text: Is that all you can say?

parts.words: Is that all you can say?
parts.note: read literally, the question asks for the whole stock of words a person is able to say, not a rebuke

explanation.surface: An exasperated retort to someone's feeble reply.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's word stock is literally everything they are able to say.

clue.text: Minister only half into religion: he should have conviction

indicators.note: into signals that the half-word goes inside the religion word

parts.note: a cult is a religious sect or system of worship

indicators.note: only half of the word for minister is used, its first three letters

parts.note: a priest is a minister of religion

explanation.surface: A clergyman only half committed to his faith ought to show stronger convictions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conviction' looks like religious belief, but the definition means a guilty verdict in court.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrongdoer is the person who ought to be found guilty in court, conviction in its legal sense.

clue.text: See struggling fencer stop, his power exhausted

indicators.note: struggling suggests the letters of these two words writhe into a new order

explanation.surface: Watch a fencer flagging, unable to stop, his strength gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is only a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes someone whose former energy or influence is used up, a person no longer effective.

clue.text: Wader gets fish, stopping hard with wings

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so these pieces fill the fish word

parts.note: the pope, or ruffe, is a small freshwater perch-like fish
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
alar is a technical adjective meaning winged or relating to wings

explanation.surface: A wading bird catches a fish, then stops hard with its wings spread.
explanation.walkthrough: The pope is an old name for the ruffe, a small perch; 'gets' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a small long-legged shore bird, one of the waders.

clue.text: Republic and province, half European

parts.note: NI, Northern Ireland, is often called the Province

indicators.note: half says only the first three of six letters are taken

parts.note: a German is a European

explanation.surface: A country and a region, partly European in character.
explanation.walkthrough: Northern Ireland is commonly called 'the Province' in Britain; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The West African state is a republic, so the general word stands for this particular example.

clue.text: Behaviour of sharks adding to growing hysteria

parts.note: feeding a fire or a fund means adding to it
a frenzy is a wild outburst of mounting agitation

explanation.surface: Sharks' conduct makes the mounting panic worse.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharks famously attack in a wild group burst when blood is in the water, the classic example of this behaviour.

clue.text: Absolutely timely, taking cue? Tremendous!

definitions.meaning: coming in exactly on cue, perfectly timed
an exclamation of hearty approval, as in great stuff

explanation.surface: An actor comes in perfectly on cue, and the director cheers.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is completed by the clue's own cue: precisely on cue means perfectly timed.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means exactly, as in exactly on time, and as a cry it is slang for excellent.

clue.text: Saga of Ibsen heroine not started

indicators.note: not started means the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: Hedda Gabler is the title heroine of Ibsen's play

explanation.surface: A story about one of Ibsen's heroines that never got going.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Norse collections of myth and heroic poetry are saga literature.

clue.text: Instrument Dudley heard at church

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: heard signals that the title is taken by its pronunciation

parts.note: Robert Dudley was Earl of Leicester, so his title stands for him

explanation.surface: A musician named Dudley is heard playing an instrument in church.
explanation.walkthrough: Dudley suggests Dudley Moore, the pianist; it is Elizabeth I's favourite Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, a title said 'Lester'. 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This keyboard instrument sounds by hammers striking steel plates, as in the Sugar Plum Fairy dance.

clue.text: Part of book leaving you cold? That's frightful

parts.note: the spine is the bound back edge of a book
something chilling makes you cold

explanation.surface: A section of a book that left the reader unmoved is declared awful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving you cold' suggests boredom, but here it is literal chilling; 'That's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Spine-tingling horror is terrifying, so frightful in its literal sense of causing fright.

clue.text: Appreciated stage revolving round one actor

indicators.note: round means the turned letters are wrapped around the numeral
revolving follows both words and turns their combined letters back to front

parts.note: dig is slang for appreciate, so appreciated is dug
a leg is a stage of a journey or race
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A theatre's revolving stage earned praise for one performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolving' turns the pair to GELGUD, and 'round' wraps that around I; the stage is a leg of a race, not a theatre, and 'dig' is slang for appreciate.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John was a celebrated English stage and screen actor.

clue.text: In Britain, refill to fly once for this?

definitions.text: In Britain, refill to fly once for this?

indicators.note: fly suggests the letters are sent in all directions into a new order

explanation.surface: A question about why Britain once refilled planes and flew them out.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the 1948-49 airlift that resupplied West Berlin by air while also being the anagram, so 'In' and 'once for this' are part of the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The Allied operation flew supplies into blockaded West Berlin, refilling the city by air, with the RAF taking part.

clue.text: Stipulated changes in boring texts

indicators.note: changes signals that the letters of the first word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Agreed revisions are written into tedious documents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Trite remarks repeated without freshness are dull pronouncements, as in a sermon of tired sayings.

clue.text: Almost the last hot drink

indicators.note: almost says the word stops one letter short

parts.note: the latter means the last of two mentioned

explanation.surface: Nearly the final drink of the evening, served hot.
explanation.definitionFit: A milky espresso coffee is served as a warm beverage.

clue.text: It's a goal not to be beaten, clubs admitted, with certain sides

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so the suit letter goes inside
beaten as in eggs beaten up suggests the letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: A football tale: it's a goal that won't be beaten, with clubs let in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be beaten' rearranges A GOAL NOT into OTAGONAL; 'admitted' puts C after the first O. 'It's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The shape has a fixed number of faces, eight, so it is defined vaguely as having a specific set of edges.

clue.text: Catch acts in play in sequence

parts.note: to take is to catch, as a ball or a fish
turns are short acts in a variety show

explanation.surface: A thief nabs performers in a show one after another.
explanation.walkthrough: A music-hall 'turn' is a single act on the bill.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing things by turns means doing them one after another, alternately in order.

clue.text: Worker in oil to sketch part of head

parts.note: a rough is a preliminary sketch
the neck is the narrow part joining the head to the body, part of the head-and-neck region

explanation.surface: A painter working in oils roughs out part of a portrait's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worker in oil' suggests an oil painter; it is a labourer on an oil rig. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A labourer on an oil rig or drilling crew is called by this name.

clue.text: So men not created, Americans believe? More or less

parts.note: un- is the prefix meaning not
the US Declaration of Independence holds that all men are created equal

explanation.surface: A sceptic doubts the American creed that all men are made the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So men' sets up the quotation; 'More or less' is not vagueness here but literally greater or smaller.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not the same in amount is either more or less than the other.

clue.text: No answer to recurring question that's appeared in exam again

indicators.note: recurring, running back, means the word is read backwards
A is the abbreviation for answer, and no answer drops it

parts.note: a teaser is a puzzling question

explanation.surface: A recurring exam question that nobody can answer has been set again.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing A from TEASER gives TESER, which 'recurring' turns round. 'to' and 'that's' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper set a second time has been set again, the sense of set as to set an exam.

clue.text: Some students met an African composer

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A group of students were introduced to an African composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedrich was the Czech nationalist composer of Ma Vlast and The Bartered Bride.

clue.text: The dawn of history?

parts.note: dawn here means the arrival of light and understanding, naming a period of history

explanation.surface: A question about where recorded time began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dawn of history' suggests prehistory, but the dawn is metaphorical: the coming of light to the mind in the 18th-century Age of Reason.
explanation.definitionFit: The 18th-century Age of Reason brought intellectual light, a figurative dawn in European history.

clue.text: Look in the eye, and shaft

definitions.meaning: a glint or bright expression in someone's eye
a beam or shaft of light

explanation.surface: Stare someone down, then wound them with a spear.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses mean a brief flash of light, one in the eye, one a beam.

clue.text: Grass skirt's bottom beginning to part

parts.note: the hem is the bottom edge of a skirt

indicators.note: beginning to means the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A grass skirt's lower edge starts to come apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass skirt' reads as one item, but 'Grass' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The fibre plant is cannabis, and grass is slang for cannabis.

clue.text: To point's impolite, it's held — so one's ' learned

parts.note: E, east, is a compass point

indicators.note: held means kept inside, so the it goes within the impolite word

parts.note: rude means impolite
the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Pointing is held to be rude, so a cultivated person knows better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' and 'so one's' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Learned here is an adjective, scholarly and well read, as in a learned professor.

clue.text: Crafty type commonly told to get bucket down

indicators.note: commonly told signals a casual, dropped-h pronunciation of the phrase

parts.note: to bucket down is to rain hard

explanation.surface: Someone is warned in local speech that it is going to pour.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken carelessly, rain hard sounds like the fox's name; 'to get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Reynard is the traditional name for the fox in fable, the proverbially cunning animal.

clue.text: Great family man simply got a break

indicators.note: break signals that the letters of these words are broken up and reformed

explanation.surface: A family man simply caught a lucky break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got a' is part of the fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A man with several wives at once has a large household, a pun on great family.

clue.text: State service

definitions.meaning: .... is the abbreviation for Massachusetts, a US state
a Catholic service of the Eucharist

explanation.surface: A two-word entry about the condition of a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: Massachusetts is shortened to the four letters, and the Eucharist is celebrated as a religious service.
